analysis.one_liner: Requires the FCC to set rules protecting callers from overcharges and tricks by telephone operator services.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a vote: it was referred to the Senate Commerce Committee in September 1989, a subcommittee held one hearing in February 1990, and it died there when the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: After AT&T was broken up, thousands of payphones in hotels, hospitals, and airports were served by private operator-service companies. Callers often could not tell who was handling their call, were quoted no price, were charged for calls they never completed, and were blocked from reaching their own long-distance company. This bill would have ordered the Federal Communications Commission to write rules within months: operators would have to identify themselves before any charge, post their rates near the phone, quote prices on request, let callers hang up free, and stop blocking callers' choice of long-distance carrier. The FCC would also have to publish every provider's rates and, if the market was not keeping prices fair, cap rates at just-and-reasonable levels. The bill was referred to the Senate Commerce Committee, a subcommittee held a hearing, and no further action was ever taken.
analysis.who_benefits: People who make phone calls from payphones in hotels, hospitals, airports, and other public places — travelers, hospital visitors, and people without home phones of their own — who would get rate disclosures, protection from charges for uncompleted calls, access to their preferred carrier, and limits on inflated per-call rates.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Payphone callers at hotels and airports

how_it_helps.text: Operators would have to identify themselves audibly before the caller incurred any charge, and callers could hang up at no charge [S3].
Providers would have to quote rates on request, disclose how charges are collected and how complaints are resolved, and post their name, address, and toll-free number on or near each payphone [S3].

Providers and the locations hosting the phones could not block callers from reaching the long-distance carrier of their choice, and locations where blocking occurred would forfeit commissions and face the FCC's lowest filed rate [S3].

Providers could not knowingly charge for uncompleted calls, could not inflate the distance a call is measured at, and could not engage in 'call splashing' — transferring a call to a pricier operator service after it originates [S3].

Every provider would have to file a public tariff of its rates and fees, and the FCC could force any provider whose rates appear unjust or unreasonable to prove they reflect reasonable cost plus a reasonable profit [S3].
The bill responded to more than 2,000 consumer complaints to the FCC between January 1988 and February 1989 about deception and blocked carrier access in operator services [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Operator-service companies would lose revenue from inflated rates, charges for uncompleted calls, and captive traffic; hotels, hospitals, airports, and payphone owners would lose commissions that partly came from those practices; some payphone equipment would have to be upgraded to allow carrier choice.

drawbacks.text: Phone sites such as hotels and hospitals earn commissions on operator calls; forfeiting commissions and routing calls to the lowest-priced carrier would cut that income, and owners argued such payments help cover the cost of maintaining payphones [S3].
Existing payphone equipment would generally have to be upgraded to support caller-chosen access codes, a real cost the FCC could waive only where benefits did not justify it [S3].

Requiring carriers to bill calling-card calls at the card issuer's rate would reduce the freedom of operator providers to set their own prices, and providers would bear new disclosure, routing, and emergency-call-handling compliance burdens [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The consumer protections are concrete and narrowly aimed at documented abuses — hidden rates, charges for uncompleted calls, and blocked carrier choice — while the costs fall mainly on the businesses profiting from those practices. The main design question is whether the FCC could keep anti-fraud waivers and equipment rules from becoming loopholes, but the bill gave the Commission flexibility on both. On balance the costs are the ordinary cost of policing a captive market.

outcome.mechanism: The bill sat in the Senate Commerce Committee after a single subcommittee hearing and never reached the Senate floor before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Alan Dixon introduced the bill on September 19, 1989, and it was read twice and referred to the Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation [S1] [S5].
Five senators — three Democrats and two Republicans — signed on as cosponsors [S4].
On February 7, 1990, the Subcommittee on Communications held a hearing on the bill (printed as S.Hrg. 101-763), but the full committee never acted on it [S5].
No further action was taken before the 101st Congress ended on January 3, 1991, so the bill died in committee without ever getting a floor vote [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Operator-service companies and the hotels, hospitals, and airports that collect commissions from them are better off: the disclosure rules, the ban on charging for uncompleted calls, and the threat of rate regulation never took effect, so callers at public phones remained captive to whatever rates and practices each provider set.

for.name: Alan J. Dixon
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and documented in its findings over 2,000 consumer complaints about operator-service practices.

for.name: Senate Subcommittee on Communications
for.what_they_did: Held a hearing on the bill on February 7, 1990 (S.Hrg. 101-763).

sides.party_line_note: Cosponsorship was bipartisan (three Democrats and two Republicans), but no vote was ever taken, so the partisan split on the bill itself cannot be measured; its death in committee is not recorded as any party's action.

industries.industry: Operator-service providers (companies handling calls from payphones at hotels, hospitals, and airports)
industries.note: The bill would end their most profitable practices: undisclosed rates, charges for uncompleted and inflated-distance calls, and blocking callers from their chosen carrier. It would also expose their full rates in public tariffs and allow the FCC to force rate reductions if the market did not keep prices fair [S3].

industries.industry: Aggregators — hotels, hospitals, airports, and other sites hosting public phones
industries.note: These sites earn commissions on the operator calls made from their premises, and the bill would forfeit those commissions wherever carrier blocking occurred and route such calls to the lowest-priced carrier. That income partly reflects rates charged to their own customers and visitors [S3].

New equipment would have to support caller-chosen carrier access codes and existing equipment would generally need upgrading, creating mandated sales but also compliance costs; the FCC could waive the rules where costs outweighed benefits [S3].

The bill would end operator-service blocking of carrier access codes and require calling-card calls to be billed at the card carrier's own rate, restoring captive traffic and rate protection to the carriers consumers actually chose [S3].
